From caring for people
to designing places

Now, as a Sustainable Urban Design engineering student, I'm bringing that perspective into a new field. I'm learning to look at streets, transport, public spaces and infrastructure not just as systems, but as places people need to navigate and belong in.

Different profession. Same curiosity about people.

Selected projects / 01

Quito: Where Landscape
Shapes the City

How volcanic ground, steep slopes, rainfall and seismic hazards influence urban development, infrastructure and everyday accessibility in Quito, Ecuador.

TypeCompleted academic research project
Assessment5/5 · Excellent
LocationQuito, Ecuador
Year2026
Field notes / Project 001

A city shaped by its terrain.

Quito stretches through a mountainous Andean landscape. Its geology and elevation influence where people build, how streets connect, and which places face environmental hazards.

For my Geography & Ecology coursework at HAMK, I examined how these physical conditions relate to sustainable urban development. This completed academic research project received a grade of 5/5. It is an environmental and urban analysis, not an engineered design proposal.

the question ↗

How can urban development respond to the landscape while remaining safer and more accessible for the people living there?

Geography & Ecology · Completed academic case study · 2026 · Grade 5/5
01 / Reading the landscape

Four forces shaping Quito

01 ✳

Volcanic ground

Volcanic deposits and hardened soils such as cangahua create varying ground conditions. Cutting slopes and removing vegetation can affect stability.

Earth materials · Site conditions
02 ⌁

Earthquakes & volcanoes

The Quito Fault System and nearby volcanoes make seismic resilience, building safety and reliable infrastructure important planning considerations.

Hazard exposure · Resilience
03 ☂

Rainfall & slopes

Steep terrain, altered drainage and heavy rainfall can combine to increase erosion, landslide and debris-flow risks.

Stormwater · Slope stability
04 ↗

Elevation & access

Two places can look close on a map yet be difficult to travel between. Steep gradients affect walking, public transport access and emergency routes.

Mobility · Inclusive planning
Sketchbook / Conceptual analysis

Distance isn't just a line on a map.

This diagram is conceptual, not a GIS map or measured accessibility analysis. It illustrates a question from my research: how does vertical distance change what it means for a destination to be “nearby”?

02 / From evidence to planning questions

What the research suggests

01

Design with the ground, not against it. Local geology, slope stability and drainage should inform decisions about development and infrastructure.

02

Plan for disruption. Seismic hazards and extreme rainfall make resilient connections, evacuation routes and infrastructure redundancy important.

03

Measure accessibility in three dimensions. Walking distance alone does not describe the experience of a steep urban route.

Personal reflection / Completed project

What I’m taking forward

This project helped me connect physical geography with everyday urban experiences. The same hillside can be a geotechnical challenge, a drainage problem, and a barrier to someone trying to reach a bus stop.

The completed research earned a grade of 5/5. It strengthened my ability to connect environmental evidence with planning decisions and everyday accessibility. As I develop my technical skills, I hope to explore these questions further through maps, GIS analysis and urban design exercises.

next iterations ✎

Terrain map · Slope and hazard layers · Accessibility analysis · Design response

Ideas for future independent extensions · Not part of the graded submission

Research foundations

Based on my HAMK Geography & Ecology coursework and its cited literature, including Alvarado et al. (2014), Chase et al. (2023), Watson et al. (2022), and Hen-Jones et al. (2026). The original academic submission contains the project references. Full bibliographic details and any source visuals should be verified before public publication.

Project role: Student research, literature review and synthesis. Status: Completed · Grade: 5/5 (Excellent).

Project 002 / Independent design study / 2026

Rautatienpuisto
Puutarhahuone.

A warm, free public place to stop, read, talk or simply breathe, in every Finnish season.

Riihimäki, FinlandUrban design conceptAccessibility firstIn development
The vision / Between the Tracks & the Trees

A public living room among the trees.

What if a historic railway park could offer a place to pause throughout the year, without requiring visitors to buy anything? This independent concept explores a Nordic heritage-inspired glasshouse surrounded by a biodiversity-focused sensory garden.

01 / People first

Belonging should be free.

01 ✳

Open to everyone

Free entry, a shared interior and no expectation to purchase anything. Visitors can rest, read, chat or enjoy the plants.

02 ↗

Accessible by design

Proposed automatic step-free doors, clear circulation, wheelchair-compatible tables and supportive chairs and benches.

03 ❋

Four-season comfort

A heated winter garden with summer shading, ventilation and planting selected for a realistic indoor climate.

04 ♧

Finnish character

Forest-green timber, a restrained pitched roof and a simple architectural language inspired by the surrounding railway-town heritage.

02 / Space planning

One room. Room for everyone.

The current spatial study explores a 12 × 7 m (84 m²) shared interior with two wheelchair-accessible tables, six supportive chairs, two fixed benches and planting concentrated around the perimeter. A separate weather-protected vestibule is proposed.

84 m²Proposed main room
2Accessible tables
6 + 2Chairs and benches
FreePublic access
03 / Design responsibility

Beautiful is only the beginning.

Accessibility

Review door operation, clear widths, approach space, table knee clearance, turning areas, slip resistance, contrast and seating ergonomics against applicable Finnish requirements.

Climate & energy

Study insulation, glazing, heat recovery, ventilation, snow loads, overheating, operating costs and long-term maintenance. A heated glass building is not automatically sustainable.

Biodiversity

Explore seasonal, pollinator-supporting planting outdoors and appropriately selected indoor greenery. Protect existing mature trees where possible.

Heritage & site fit

Verify park boundaries, existing paths and vegetation, heritage restrictions, utilities, planning rules and the suitability of any proposed building location.

Project status / Ongoing independent work

Concept established. Research next.

This project was developed as a remote, desktop-based design exercise. The illustrations communicate intent; they do not document an existing building or demonstrate a permit-ready, accessible or structurally verified solution.

Next steps include mapping the real site, checking Finnish accessibility guidance and planning constraints, refining the floor plan and assessing year-round energy use.

the idea ↗

A public space should offer more than a route from one place to another. Sometimes its most important purpose is giving people somewhere to stop and breathe.

About me

Hi, I'm Daniela Turunen.

I’m an engineering student, a curious observer of everyday places, and someone who believes accessibility should be part of the first sketch, not the final checklist.

Outside the classroom

I find inspiration outdoors, on walks and hikes, and in the everyday details of places. I’m interested in how a space feels to move through, not only how it looks on a plan.

✳ Nature observer↗ Curious by default⌁ Human-centered design✎ Always learning

From healthcare to the built environment

Before studying Sustainable Urban Design at Häme University of Applied Sciences (HAMK), I trained and worked as a practical nurse. Healthcare taught me to notice the small, everyday barriers that can make independence, movement and participation harder than they need to be.

That experience sparked a wider curiosity: what if we thought about accessibility and human needs much earlier, when planning streets, public spaces, transport and infrastructure? Engineering gives me a new set of tools to explore that question.

I am still at the beginning of my engineering journey. This portfolio is a place to share what I am learning, the questions I am asking, and the projects that help me connect technical knowledge with real human experiences.

My approach

People first. Always curious.

I’m drawn to the details that shape everyday life: a crossing that feels safe, a route that actually works, or a public space where more people feel welcome. I want to understand the technical decisions behind those experiences.
